title: MacWhisper vs Wispr Flow on Mac in 2026: which one fits your voice work
metaTitle: MacWhisper vs Wispr Flow on Mac: files or live dictation?
description: MacWhisper vs Wispr Flow compared on price, privacy and platforms. See which Mac app fits file transcription and which fits dictation in any app.
intro: MacWhisper turns audio and video files into text on your Mac, and its Pro license is a one-time €64. Wispr Flow dictates into any app and sells monthly or annual plans, with a free tier of 2,000 words per week. Pick the app that matches the job you do most, not the one you have heard more about.
tldr: MacWhisper is a file-first transcription app. Its Pro license is a one-time €64 per license on macwhisper.com.
Wispr Flow is a dictation app for Mac, Windows, iOS and Android. Pro is $12 per user per month on annual billing.
Pick MacWhisper for recordings you already have. Pick Wispr Flow for speaking into any app.
Lazur is a third option, a voice assistant that sees your screen. Dictation is included, but it is not the headline.

blocks.text: If you need to turn recordings into text on a Mac, MacWhisper is the better tool. If you need to speak into the app you already use, Wispr Flow is built for that. The two overlap less than most comparisons suggest. MacWhisper works on files you already have. Wispr Flow works in the text box in front of you.
What each app is built to do

MacWhisper comes from Good Snooze. Its site says it uses local models to transcribe your files, so sensitive recordings can stay on your Mac. The feature list centers on files. You get batch transcription, subtitle export in .srt and .vtt, and export to .txt, .md, .pdf, .html and .docx. It also records meetings, watches folders and connects to workflow integrations.

Wispr Flow is a dictation product. Its homepage describes dictation in any app with no plugins. It removes filler words and self-corrections, keeps a personal vocabulary, and supports snippets and writing styles in 100+ languages. Its Notetaker records meetings on Mac or Windows and writes transcripts with named speakers and summaries.

Lazur is a third option, and a different kind of tool. It is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Hold fn to dictate clean text at the cursor. Dictation is included, but it is not the headline.
MacWhisper vs Wispr Flow pricing: one payment or a monthly bill

MacWhisper's site lists a free tier and a Pro license. The free tier is €0 per month and free forever. Pro is a one-time €64 per license, and that includes lifetime updates. The Gumroad listing did not show a price when it was checked. Confirm the price on that page before you pay.

A competing review lists a different price for the App Store version, at $6.99 per month, $29.99 per year or $99.99 lifetime. It calls the two versions confusingly different products. That review is opinion from a dictation rival, so verify prices yourself. Buy the version you actually need.

blocks.text: Do the math before you choose. Wispr Pro on annual billing is $12 per user per month, or $144 for a year. MacWhisper Pro is €64 once. A competing review puts that near $69. At the annual rate, Wispr Pro passes that amount within about six months. That does not make MacWhisper the better deal. It means you pay for different things.

Currency matters too. MacWhisper prices in euros on its own site, and Wispr prices in dollars. Exchange rates move. Compare the two in one currency on the day you buy, and check whether your card adds foreign transaction fees.
MacWhisper vs Wispr Flow for dictation or file transcription

This is the split that matters most. MacWhisper is primarily a file tool. A competing review calls it primarily a file-transcription tool, not a real-time dictation app. That is opinion, but it matches the feature list on macwhisper.com, which leads with files.

Wispr Flow works the other way. It listens while you talk and places clean text where your cursor sits. You do not need a plugin for each app. That matters when you write all day in Mail, Slack or Notes, and you want the text to land in the box you already have open.

items: MacWhisper: you have an audio or video file and need text, subtitles or a Word file.
MacWhisper: you want to process a folder of recordings as one batch.
Wispr Flow: you want to talk into email, chat or documents without switching apps.
Wispr Flow: you need notes from a live meeting with speaker names on Mac or Windows.

blocks.text: Edge cases that change the answer

Speaker labels are the first edge case. MacWhisper's speaker diarization is in beta, according to a competing review. If you need reliable speaker names in an interview transcript, test one real file before you buy. Wispr's Notetaker advertises named speakers for meetings, so the two tools solve different speaker problems.

Language is the second edge case. Wispr lists 100+ languages for dictation. The MacWhisper material I read did not give a language count, so check that your language is supported before you commit to a long recording. A closer microphone almost always helps any transcription tool. Plug in a headset or a lapel mic for interviews.
Privacy: where your audio goes in each app

MacWhisper says it uses local models to transcribe files, and that sensitive content can stay on your Mac. Its site does not mention telemetry or analytics. That is not the same as saying none exists, so read its privacy policy too. If you bring your own AI provider API keys, your data goes to that provider. Read that provider's terms before you connect it.

Wispr Flow's privacy page says your data is never sold. It says turning off training means nothing you say is used to train its models. Audio is deleted as soon as it is transcribed, unless you turn on Dictation cloud storage. Wispr Flow is a cloud product. Its homepage claims SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 and HIPAA compliance. Those are company claims, and the site links no independent audit report.

blocks.title: Check the training setting
blocks.text: A competing review says model training is on by default on Free and Pro plans. Wispr's privacy page says you can turn it off. Open Wispr Flow's data and privacy settings and check the toggle yourself before you dictate client or medical content.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer you. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. If your work involves protected data, read each provider's policy before you start.
MacWhisper vs Wispr Flow on Mac, Windows and iPhone

MacWhisper is a Mac app, and reviews call it Mac-only. Its site does not state a macOS version for the direct version. A competing review says the App Store version needs macOS 15 or later and iOS 18 or later. The App Store build is a separate product from the Gumroad license, so check which one you are getting.

Wispr Flow dictation runs on Mac, Windows, iOS and Android. Its Notetaker runs on Mac and Windows only. If you dictate on your iPhone and your Mac, turn on dictation cloud storage. Your history then shows up on all your devices. That is the trade for cross-device use.

The free tier is the first limit you hit. Wispr's homepage says 2,000 words per week. At 220 words per minute, the speed one competing reviewer measured, that is about nine minutes of speech. That reviewer also said they burned through the free limit within two to three days. Real use varies, but heavy users hit the cap fast.
Set up each app in your first hour

Start with permissions. Open System Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone and turn on the apps you plan to use. Some dictation tools also ask for Accessibility access so they can type into other apps. Check that list too.

Then run one real task. For MacWhisper, drop in a short recording you already know the answer to. For Wispr Flow, dictate one email reply. For Lazur, hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask about something on screen. If you want a rough sense of your own speed, try the [speaking vs typing test](/tools/speaking-vs-typing-test) first.
Worked examples: three jobs you might have this week

Say you have a 70 minute interview recording from a podcast. Drop the file into MacWhisper, pick a model size, and let it run on your Mac. Export the transcript as .docx for editing, and export .srt if you need captions. Wispr Flow is the wrong tool for this job, because its listed features cover dictation and meeting notes, not batch files.

Now say you answer dozens of Slack messages and a handful of emails each day. You want your voice in the text box, with the filler words removed. Wispr Flow fits that job. Click into the box, use its dictation shortcut, speak, and check the text. Watch the free limit first. At 2,000 words a week, a busy inbox runs out early.

Now say you are in an app you have never used, and you cannot find the export menu. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask where it is. Lazur draws a circle and a label around the control. Lazur does not click it for you. Ask Lazur to walk you through it, and it waits for each click. That is a different job from either transcription app.
Mistakes people make when they compare these two apps

items: Buying MacWhisper for live dictation. Its strength is files. Test any live use with a short clip before you pay.
Assuming the Gumroad and App Store versions match. A competing review calls them confusingly different products.
Paying Wispr Flow monthly out of habit. The pricing page shows $12 per user on annual billing against $15 monthly.
Dictating client or medical content before you check the training and storage settings.
Expecting Lazur to replace a transcription app. Its listed features cover screen help, voice actions and dictation, not batch files.
Skipping the free tier. Run one real task in each app before you choose a paid plan.

blocks.text: Where each app is better, stated fairly

MacWhisper is the better buy for recordings. Its one-time price avoids a subscription. Reviewers praise its on-device transcription accuracy, especially with larger Whisper models, and its batch file handling. The same review calls speaker diarization beta and notes no Windows, Linux or Android support. Those are opinions from a dictation rival. Weigh them as opinions.

Wispr Flow is the better buy for dictation across devices. A competing reviewer calls it one of the most polished AI dictation tools available right now. Its cleanup removes filler words and self-corrections. Its Growth plan adds SSO with SAML and org-wide HIPAA enforcement with a signed BAA. Its downsides are real. There is no offline mode, and the free tier is small.

Lazur is the better buy when you want help inside whatever app is open. It can answer questions about what is on screen, point at controls, and run voice actions. Those include timers, Apple Reminders, Calendar events, music and volume, opening apps and links, web search and Shortcuts. It can also run research in its own Chrome tabs and return a summary and report. It is not a transcription suite.
What to do next before you pay

items: Write down the job. Is it files, live dictation, or help inside apps?
Run the free tier or trial for one real task. Use a real recording or a real inbox.
Check the live pricing page for each app, then compare in one currency.
Read the privacy and training settings for your content type before you upload anything sensitive.
If you are weighing Lazur too, read [Lazur vs MacWhisper](/compare/lazur-vs-macwhisper) or [Lazur vs Wispr Flow](/compare/lazur-vs-wispr-flow).

blocks.text: Start with the job, not the brand. A transcript, a dictation habit and an on-screen helper need different tools. Some people end up needing two of them, and that is fine.

faq.question: Is MacWhisper or Wispr Flow better on Mac?
faq.answer: It depends on the job. MacWhisper is better for transcribing files you already have, with batch jobs and subtitle export. Wispr Flow is better for dictating into any app, with cleanup of filler words. Neither replaces the other in every case.

faq.question: Does Wispr Flow work offline?
faq.answer: A competing review says Wispr Flow has no offline mode, so transcription is cloud-based. Wispr's privacy page describes how audio is handled after transcription. Test dictation without a connection before you rely on it while travelling.

faq.question: Does MacWhisper work offline?
faq.answer: MacWhisper says it uses local models to transcribe your files, so files can stay on your Mac. If you add your own AI provider API keys, data goes to that provider. The site does not describe offline dictation, so test that part before you need it.

faq.question: Which costs less, MacWhisper or Wispr Flow?
faq.answer: MacWhisper Pro is a one-time €64 per license on macwhisper.com. Wispr Pro is $12 per user per month on annual billing, or $15 monthly. A competing review puts the MacWhisper price near $69, and Wispr passes that within about six months. Compare in one currency on the day you buy.

faq.question: Does Wispr Flow use my dictation to train its AI?
faq.answer: Wispr's privacy page says you can turn training off, and that nothing you say is used to train its models once you do. A competing review says training is on by default on Free and Pro plans. Check the setting in Wispr Flow before you dictate sensitive content.

faq.question: Can Lazur replace MacWhisper or Wispr Flow?
faq.answer: Not for every job. Lazur is a voice assistant that sees your screen, answers out loud and runs voice actions. Dictation is included with fn. Its listed features do not include batch file transcription, so keep a transcription app for recordings.

faq.question: Is there a free way to try these apps?
faq.answer: MacWhisper lists a free tier at €0 per month, free forever, and does not list its limits. Wispr Flow's free tier allows 2,000 words per week. Lazur has a 3-day Pro trial that starts when you first open the app, with no credit card.

verdict: Pick MacWhisper if your work starts with a recording and ends with a transcript, and you want to pay once. Pick Wispr Flow if you speak into email, chat and documents on more than one device, and you can accept cloud processing and a small free tier. Pick Lazur if you want help inside the app you already have, with dictation as a bonus. Many Mac users will use one transcription app and never need the other two.
